newsitem.title: INDIA: India Hind Lever working on new detergent.
newsitem.headline: India Hind Lever working on new detergent.

text.p: Unilever's Indian subsidiary Hindustan Lever Ltd (HLL) is working on a new detergent aimed at sharply reducing the quantity of water used to wash clothes, a company official said on Friday.
"Imagine a detergent using half the (amount of) water," M.S. Banga, HLL director, told a business meeting. "It could double our income, given our water shortage."
He said HLL was working on such a detergent but did not give any further details. Banga was speaking about the technological challenges and the market scenario by the turn of the century.
HLL is India's leading soaps and detergents maker.
"The nation and consumers are getting richer," he said. This would translate to excellent marketing opportunities in urban and rural India, he said.
He said India was heading for a demographical transformation with a sharp rise in the number of people below the age of 25 by the turn of the century.

They will be educated and sophisticated, sceptical and more demanding. "They won't buy Lux because of recommendations by film stars," he said, referring to HLL's Lux brand of soap and the use of celebrities to promote it.
The new breed of confident and aggressive consumer would be quick to try out new products and quick to drop them too, Banga said.

Indian companies would have to graduate from reactive marketing to predictive marketing in the coming years. He said new entrants would take to direct home selling to break big firms' stranglehold of distribution network.
"In the past, success came from being efficient," Banga said. "In the future, it will come from the ability to build (create) new markets."
Banga said the Indian market will continue to show a pyramid shape, with low priced mass volume products at the bottom and low volume premium products at the top.
A sharp increase in the number of upper income groups would trigger the launch of many more premium products. "And unlike in the past, they won't struggle for survival," he said.
Banga said the coming years would ring warning bells for large successful companies including his own.
"New ways of doing business are seldom invented by big companies -- but mostly by new entrants," he told the meeting.
